His body was still small, but his paws were as big as bear's claws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma was still standing upright in front of the kitchen bench.
She gazed at the dog for a long time.

He was certain that death would not snatch life from him, but would gently take it from his hand.

To which Bauer Häubel, of course, would answer yes.

He would apologize in advance for the coldness of his hands, which he knew wouldn't bother Farmer Häubel at all, and then he would put a hand over Farmer Häubel's eyes.
The people in the village were upset; it was evident, even though they were mostly trying not to show it.

This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, people in the village were acting as if black ice had formed on all their paths, not only outside but also inside their homes, with black ice in the kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as though their own bodies were entirely alien to them, as though all their joints were inflamed and even the objects they handled were extremely combustible.
All day long, they viewed their life and, as far as possible, everyone else's with suspicion.
Again and again they looked back to check if there was someone coming after them with lethal intent; someone who had lost their mind and therefore had nothing notable left to lose.
And they quickly looked ahead again, because after all, someone without reason could attack from the front as well.
They looked up to rule out any falling roof tiles, branches or heavy lamp shades.
They avoided all animals, because they believed that it could break out faster from them than from humans.

They made a wide berth around the usually gentle cows, which might be inclined to kick today; they avoided the dogs too, even the really old ones that could hardly stand but might still go for their throats today.
On such days, anything was possible; even a decrepit dachshund could rip your throat out that wasn't any more far-fetched than an okapi.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, most of the villagers were generally not superstitious.
They carelessly did all the things that are not to be done in superstition:

They sat calmly under wall clocks, even though superstition can cause death from it; they slept with their heads towards the door, although in superstition that means you'll be carried out feet first through the same door soon.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's, which, as Elsbeth warned, in superstition is equivalent to suicide or abetting a murder.
They were not startled when the owl hooted in the night, when a horse in the stable was drenched in sweat, or when a dog howled with its head bowed low.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, there were no stops in between.
Since our first train journey, we always played the same game:
We would stand with our backs to the windows at the opposite train doors.
Martin would close his eyes, while I watched out of the train door that Martin had his back to.
In the first class, I had listed to Martin everything I saw during the journey, and Martin tried to memorize it all.

This worked out very well, so by the second year of school, I no longer needed to enumerate things and Martin, with his back to the window and eyes closed, could almost recite everything I saw through the foggy train window.

She had awoken in a start, sitting upright in bed after the image of the okapi had withdrawn.
She stared at her nightdress, in which she had been standing in Uhlheck in her dreams just a moment ago, and then at the alarm clock.
Three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take this too seriously," Selma said, but she said it like a TV detective who doesn't take an anonymous letter too seriously.

I asked.
"Nothing," Selma chimed, opening the fridge, she took out a packet of sliced cheese and some liver sausage and waved them both in the air.
"Little mouse," she cooed after him, and the cooing and "little mouse" were truly alarming.
"Cheese, please," I said, "what do you have?"
"Nothing," Selma trilled, "I already told you.
She spread butter on a slice of bread, and because she was still flailing about, she knocked the cheese off the counter with her wrist.
Now Selma stood still, looking down at the package of cheese as if it were something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamt of an Okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards.
Therefore, we were convinced that dreaming of an Okapi and death were irrevocably linked.
That's how our mind works.

For example, coffee pots and shoelaces, or deposit bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs at Selma's, she would tell me stories with happy endings at the bedside.
When I was younger, after the stories, I would always grasp her wrist, place my thumb on her pulse and imagine that the entire world was moving to the rhythm of Selma's heartbeat.

I imagined the optician grinding lenses, Martin lifting a weight, Elsbeth trimming her hedge, the retailer stacking juice bags, my mother piling up fir branches, my father stamping prescriptions all of them doing so exactly in time with Selma's heartbeat.
I used to always fall asleep reliably to this, but now, at ten years old, Selma thought I was too old for it.
